sessions.title: The Need for Preemptive Scheduling in Microsecond-scale Systems
sessions.listing_title: The Need for Preemptive Scheduling in Microsecond-scale Systems
sessions.description:
Most recently proposed user-level stacks and network
dataplanes for micro-second scale applications, use
non-preemptive policies to schedule requests to cores.
For the many real-world scenarios where protocol
processing and request service times follow
distributions with high dispersion or a heavy tail,
they allow short requests to be blocked behind long
requests (head of line blocking), which leads to poor
tail latency and suboptimal throughput.

This talk will argue that preemptive scheduling is not
only compatible with microsecond-scale latencies, it is
necessary. To illustrate this point, we will describe
Shinjuku a single-address space runtime system that
uses hardware support for virtualization to make
preemption practical at the microsecond scale. This
allows Shinjuku to implement centralized scheduling
policies that preempt requests as often as every 5μsec
and work well for both light and heavy tailed request
service time distributions. We demonstrate that
Shinjuku provides significant tail latency and
throughput improvements previously proposed dataplanes
for a wide range of workload scenarios.For the case of
a RocksDB server processing both point and range
queries, Shinjuku achieves up to 6.6× higher throughput
and 88% lower tail latency.

This talk will draw heavily from our experience in
building low latency runtime systems (Dune @ OSDI'10,
IX @ OSDI'14, Shinjuku @ NSDI'18). As we strive to
achieve low latency for a wider range of workloads, we
move towards more general scheduling capabilities.
Hence, a number of key questions arise: can a single
runtime system or a single policy work well across all
cases? what and where is the boundary between network
protocol processing and application code? are we slowly
rebuilding full-featured operating system kernels? what
are the key lessons that can inform the kernel's
development to better support microsecond-scale RPC
systems? The talk will touch on these questions.

sessions.title: Potential IPv4 Unicast Expansions
sessions.listing_title: Potential IPv4 Unicast Expansions
sessions.description:
IPv4's success story was in carrying unicast packets
worldwide.
Service sites still need IPv4 addresses for everything,
since the majority of Internet client nodes don't yet
have IPv6 addresses. IPv4 addresses now cost 15 to 20
dollars apiece (times the size of your network!) and
the price is rising.

The IPv4 address space includes hundreds of millions of
addresses reserved for obscure (the ranges 0/8, and
127/16), or obsolete (225/8-231/8) reasons, or for
"future use" (240/4 - otherwise known as class E).
Instead of leaving these IP addresses unused, we have
started an effort to make them usable, generally. This
work stalled out 10 years ago, because IPv6 was going
to be universally deployed by now, and reliance on IPv4
was expected to be much lower than it in fact still is.

We have been reporting bugs and sending patches to
various vendors. For Linux, we have patches accepted
in the kernel and patches pending for the
distributions, routing daemons, and userland tools.
Slowly but surely, we are decontaminating these IP
addresses so they can be used in the near future.

Many routers already handle many of these addresses,
or can easily be configured to do so, and so we are
working to expand unicast treatment of these addresses
in routers and other OSes. We plan an authorized
experiment to route some of these addresses globally,
monitor their reachability from different parts of the
Internet, and talk to ISPs who are not yet treating
them as unicast to update their networks.

Wouldn't it be a better world with a few hundred
million more IPv4 addresses in it?

sessions.title: Implementing the Next Generation of Network Telemetry Technologies
sessions.listing_title: Implementing the Next Generation of Network Telemetry Technologies
sessions.description:
Current network monitoring and telemetry applications
require host-based collectors across all nodes in a
network (both on servers/hypervisors and traditional
switches and routers). These can be effective
solutions, but just as datacenter deployment patterns
have evolved new technology to track traffic as it
moves through the network had emerged. Newer
specifications like INT[1] and IFA[2] propose standards
to add metadata to packets or clone and add metadata as
they flow through a network to allow collectors/agents
to gather data at the network edges. Hardware that
supports INT/IFA can add metadata automatically with
application/flow-level/virtual-port granularity which
allows more detailed network monitoring and assurance
to customers that service levels for applications are
being met.

This talk will cover:
      
Introduction to INT and IFA network elements including
currently proposed on-wire frame formats

Hardware requirements/implementations for handling
IFA/INT today and the challenges facing those wanting
to implement them in hardware and software

Proposals for configuring INT/IFA in both software
dataplane and hardware dataplane environments on
supported hardware.

Assessing and minimizing risk associated with the
maintenance of deploying an early draft of a standard.

[1]  https://p4.org/assets/INT-current-spec.pdf
[2]  https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-kumar-ippm-ifa/

sessions.title: Accelerating QUIC via Hardware Offloads Through a Socket Interface
sessions.listing_title: Accelerating QUIC via Hardware Offloads Through a Socket Interface
sessions.description:
QUIC protocol stacks currently implemented in user
space cannot benefit from offloads like older protocols
such as TCP. An interface is needed to support hardware
offloads, such as cryptography and transmit
segmentation. This paper proposes a QUIC offload
interface that implements a new upper layer socket
protocol, similar to KTLS, which allows the QUIC stack
to enable hardware offloads and manage security
association information via socket options. Metadata is
exchanged via cmsg headers. This interface can be
easily refactored to be generic enough to support other
offloads.

Offloading IPsec crypto and transmit segmentation lead
to significant CPU utilization reduction. This paper
presents improvements achieved by offloading AES-GCM
encryption and decryption, along with segmentation for
QUIC traffic. We tested the Chromium stack with
bidirectional traffic. Offloading crypto resulted in a
10% reduction in CPU utilization. We expect CPU
utilization to reduce by ~20% with crypto and
segmentation offloaded.

The benefits of offloading crypto and segmentation for
QUIC traffic are promising. Establishing a standard
interface to enable and configure these offloads will
lead to a higher rate of adoption of hardware
solutions, reduce the cost of deployment, and
accelerate the adoption of QUIC.

sessions.title: TCP SO_TIMESTAMPING with OPT_STATS for performance analytics
sessions.listing_title: TCP SO_TIMESTAMPING with OPT_STATS for performance analytics
sessions.description:
Existing debugging and troubleshooting methods (such as
aggregate TCP statistics or opportunistic packet
captures) often fall short when debugging the
performance of individual requests and responses over
TCP, which is essential for discovering and fixing tail
latency issues in highly distributed applications. This
is because one needs the state of TCP and the lifetime
of the packets of a given application payload in the
kernel stack to deconstruct the performance
characteristics and breakdown of that payload.

Many applications and protocols use structured messages
(e.g., RPC request and response). There, we care about
the latency of each message instead of an aggregate
flow completion time. The streaming nature of TCP makes
it difficult to measure the latency and performance of
individual messages. Moreover, associating the internal
states to individual message via existing TCP_INFO
socket option is difficult and often misleading, due to
the asynchronous nature of the socket API.

In this presentation, we present how Linux kernel
timestamps can be employed to track individual messages
in the kernel networking stack, for the purpose of
performance debugging and analysis. As a crucial
extension, we also present how we can accurately
capture the state of TCP using OPT_STATS for individual
message. Further, we enumerate challenges, shortcomings
and gotchas of kernel timestamps when deployed at
scale.

sessions.title: V-switch Live-migration Support For Virtio With SRIOV VF Datapath
sessions.listing_title: V-switch Live-migration Support For Virtio With SRIOV VF Datapath
sessions.description:
Recently (in kernel 4.18) the virtio guest driver was
extended to use vf datapath, which was a step forward
to enable live-migration for virtual-machines using
virtual network functions. Under this setup, the virtio
guest driver uses the vf channel when available for the
vm and switches to use the para-virtual channel
otherwise.

This talks deals with the v-switch host side of live
migration for sriov VMs.

We propose a design based on the switchdev mode for nic
host drivers where bonding/teaming instance is set over
the host side e-switch representation endpoints for
both channels and the bond is being set as a port in
the v-switch SW model.

The design includes stitching a 2nd network function
(can be vf or a lighter nic hw function) to the
para-virtual backend, such that the host side bond is
made from the representor of the vf which is passed to
the VM and the 2nd HW function which resides in the
host.

This is essential in order to address network v-switch
flows where the vm under live-migration is the
destination and also the case of hybrid setups which
include para-virtual only or sriov only VMs.

sessions.title: Demystifying The TC Ugly (or Universal) 32bit Key Packet Classifier
sessions.listing_title: Demystifying The TC Ugly (or Universal) 32bit Key Packet Classifier
sessions.description:
The u32 classifier - invented by Alexey Kuznetsov - is
possibly the most extensible, and depending on your
usage, the most performant classifier in Linux.

The u32 classifier is the only one amongst kernel
native classifiers that can be taught by a user
policy "how to" classify based on user traffic
heuristics.
U32 uses packet Offset-Length-Value against defined
policies makes it very "hardware friendly" and well
suited for offloading.

U32 is very likely the most popular tc classifier
based on documentation we have scanned on the net.
Yet to many it still remains mysterious beyond its
basic usage.
With power comes complexity. And complexity breeds
myths; on the internet myths result in bad
documentation. We hope to rectify that situation
with this talk.

In this talk we are going to:

- Describe the basic and advanced features of
the u32 classifier
- Expose the flexibility on how one can customize it
for specific setups. We will show customization:
 + a small LAN(a few hundred users) use case
 + a large enteprise level network (10s of thousands
   of users).
- Provide numbers showing performance of the small
LAN and larger enteprise
- Illustrate how to do basic offload a u32 to the
Intel ixgbe hardware.

sessions.title: Shenango: Achieving High CPU Efficiency for Latency-sensitive Datacenter Workloads
sessions.listing_title: Shenango: Achieving High CPU Efficiency for Latency-sensitive Datacenter Workloads
sessions.description:
Datacenter applications demand microsecond-scale tail
latencies and high request rates from operating
systems, and most applications handle loads that have
high variance over multiple timescales. Achieving
these goals in a CPU-efficient way is an open problem.
Because of the high overheads of today’s kernels, the
best available solution to achieve microsecond-scale
latencies is kernel-bypass networking, which dedicates
CPU cores to applications for spin-polling the network
card. But this approach wastes CPU: even at modest
average loads, one must dedicate enough cores for the
peak expected load.

Shenango achieves comparable latencies but at far
greater CPU efficiency. It reallocates cores across
applications at very fine granularity every
5μs—enabling cycles unused by latency-sensitive
applications to be used productively by batch
processing applications. It achieves such fast
reallocation rates with:

1. an efficient algorithm that detects when
applications would benefit from more cores, and

2. a privileged component called the IOKernel that
runs on a dedicated core, steering packets from the
NIC and orchestrating core reallocations.

When handling latency-sensitive applications, such as
memcached, we found that Shenango achieves tail latency
and throughput comparable to ZygOS, a state-of-the-art,
kernel-bypass network stack, but can linearly trade
latency-sensitive application throughput for batch
processing application throughput, vastly increasing
CPU efficiency.

sessions.title: Paced Chirping - Rethinking TCP start-up
sessions.listing_title: Paced Chirping - Rethinking TCP start-up
sessions.description:
We have created a start-up algorithm called Paced
Chirping for getting a flow up to speed fast without
causing significant queueing delay. It is a promising
step towards solving slow starts dilemma between
accelerating fast and causing queueing delay. It is
purely delay based, and should therefore be applicable
to the general Internet.

Paced Chirping is a replacement of slow start that
continuously pulses the queue with groups of packets
called 'chirps'. The decreasing inter-packet gap of the
chirps allows the sender to estimate the available
capacity from queueing delay measurements. Each chirp
creates a small measurable queue, and the queue is
allowed to drain in-between subsequent chirps. Using
the capacity estimates Paced Chirping transition to
congestion avoidance without overshooting capacity.

Paced Chirping is implemented in the Linux kernel
using the internal pacing framework to realise chirps.
We have added code to the pacing framework that allows
a congestion control module to create chirps with
desired characteristics. This does allow for more
elaborate start-up schemes, made necessary by
increasing capacity. Pacing precision is a challenge
at high speed due to timing precision. With the
proposed NIC API change essayed by Van Jacobson at
netdev 0x12[1] precision can be improved significantly.

Paced Chirping achieves fast acceleration with
virtually no queueing delay, and it is a promising step
towards a start-up algorithm that can reach utilization
fast without hurting latency-sensitive applications.

sessions.title: Making the Linux TCP stack more extensible with eBPF
sessions.listing_title: Making the Linux TCP stack more extensible with eBPF
sessions.description:
We propose a novel way of extending the Linux TCP stack
by leveraging Lawrence Brakmo's TCP-BPF framework.
We implement new eBPF callbacks to support user-defined
TCP options. We present 4 use cases:

- the TCP User Timeout Option, which has been
standardized in RFC 5482 but not yet implemented in the
Linux kernel.

- Since RFC 6994, TCP supports experimental options.
We use eBPF to implement a new experimental option
that enables a client to request a server to use a
specific congestion control scheme or set the initial
congestion window. We also demonstrate how eBPF code
can be used to tune the acknowledgment strategy.

- MPTCP is another interesting use case for eBPF with
its scheduler and path manager. We present an
eBPF-based prototype MPTCP path-manager framework
and use it to implement the two existing ndiffports
and fullmesh path managers as eBPF programs.

sessions.title: Improved syscall batching for network I/O
sessions.listing_title: Improved syscall batching for network I/O
sessions.description:
Network applications can benefit from reduced CPU
cycles by amortizing the system call overhead of
network I/O operations. 
We review two existing interfaces for network I/O
batching namely recvmmsg()/sendmmsg() and SO_RCVLOWAT
and propose extensions to these mechanisms.
We found an 8x syscall reduction with our traffic
patterns (gaming scenarios) with the usage of such
extensions.

Existing recvmmsg() and sendmmsg() allow an application
to receive and send multiple messages from a socket
using a single system call. The batching performance is
dependent on how much data can be batched on the same
socket. We introduce two new APIs recvmmmsg() and
sendmmmsg() (note the extra m) which allows for
receiving and sending multiple messages from "multiple
sockets" using a single system call. These extensions
allow improved batching performance since data across
sockets can be batched in the same syscall. Apart from
the kernel changes, we explain the application layer
changes required to support these extensions.

SO_RCVLOWAT specifies the minimum amount of data that
is buffered in the socket layer before it is passed to
the application. However, if the amount of data
received is less than the specified threshold, the data
will never be passed to the application. We propose a
solution to this in the form of SO_RCVLOWAT_TIMEOUT
which allows opportunistic batching of network reads
while ensuring that buffered data is passed to the
application on timeout.

Use-cases for our extensions:
---------------------------------------------------------

- TCP proxy with multiple client connections. TCP proxy
waits on messages from multiple sockets at the same
time and may receive EPOLLIN events on multiple socket
descriptors at the same time.

- Multi-path transports where you can send the same
message on multiple sockets at the same time. Consider
MP-QUIC implementation which operates multiple paths in
redundant modes i.e. the same messages get replicated
over multiple UDP sockets.
recvmmsg()/sendmmsg() can work only with a single
socket at a time i.e. receive multiple messages on the
same socket at a time. Iterating over recvmmsg() over
multiple sockets in user-space causes considerable
syscall penalty.

Our deployment scenario
---------------------------------------------------------

We were developing multi-path UDP scheme for gaming
applications. Individual connections do not have much
data-rate but there are lots of such connections to be
handled on server. Now in our case recvmmsg()
efficiency was very low because it could not
sufficiently batch enough messages (because of low data
rate per connection). The messages are spread out over
different sockets. Similarly, in the send-side, we had
to send the same message on multiple sockets (i.e.
redundancy mode to ensure best gaming latency).
Sendmmsg() could not be used because it works only with
a single socket. Iterating over multiple sockets in
userspace is costly because of syscall overhead.
Thus we knew iterating over multiple sockets in
kernel-space is more efficient and provides lower
syscall overhead.

Performance observations
---------------------------------------------------------

- recvmmsg() actually performs worse than recvmsg(), if
the number of messages handled in the same call is
less. This is because of the additional book keeping
recvmmsg() needs to do to handle msgvec (message
vectors).

- With recvmmmsg(), the message batch size improves
drastically since there is a good probability of
multiple packets arriving over multiple sockets than on
single socket.

Sample performance figures
---------------------------------------------------------

Scenario (gaming traffic): Server waiting on 19 UDP
ports and every port receives 100K packets with
inter-packet delay of 1ms. We compare recv(),
recvmsg(), recvmmsg() with recvmmmsg(). We observe,
reduction in syscalls from 190K to 24K in case of
recvmmmsg(). With current recvmmsg() the reduction in
syscall is negligible from 190K to 189K. We have
corresponding number for CPU cycles and instruction
counts as well for all four recv primitives.

Patches to existing applications?
---------------------------------------------------------

- For mmmsg(), we have developed it as part of internal
servers employing mp-udp. We have not tested or applied
patch on any publically available application.

- For SO_RCVLOWAT_TIMEOUT extension, we have patched
libcurl. We have data with libcurl with sample file
transfer which shows syscall reduction. For 10MB file
transfer with the RCVLOWAT buffer set to 1MB with 1sec
TIMEOUT, the reduction in cpu cycles is 65%. Will cover
the data in detail in the talk, if accepted.

Error Handling with these extensions
---------------------------------------------------------

Yes we had considered error-handling and it does get
slightly complicated. For errno handling, we had to add
an additional output param in the mmmsg() syscall. The
errno information has to be reported on per socket
descriptor basis and thus the need for number of param
extension.

There is an implementation complexity for extending
syscall args beyond 6 parameters. Currently any syscall
in kernel can handle max 6 args (SYSCALL_DEFINE6(…)) .
Recvmmsg() uses 5 args but recvmmmsg() requires 7 args.
In our implementation, we have reused one parameter as
in and out and is not very user-friendly. In the
future, we would like to discuss about this on the vger
ML.

Regarding blocking/non-blocking sockets in the same fd
set, user will get what he requested. That is if the
user has included a blocking socket in the mmmsg() call
then it would block. But one point to be noted here,
that if the user calls recvmmmsg() in response to an
EPOLLIN event then this won’t be a problem, because
there is an event waiting on the fd and it won’t block.
Usually the user will prepare a “set of descriptors” on
which EPOLLIN event was received and pass them to
recvmmmsg() api. Even in case of LOWAT, the EPOLLIN
event will be generated only when the descriptor has
data (as per what is set in the LOWAT).

sessions.title: End-to-end networking with ILNP in Linux
sessions.listing_title: End-to-end networking with ILNP in Linux
sessions.description:
The Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP) is
defined as an Experimental Internet Protocol by the
Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) in RFCs 6740-6748.
At the heart of the ILNP architecture is a radical
approach to addressing for the Internet:
the deprecation of IP addresses, to be replaced
by the use of node Identifiers and network Locators.

The key benefits of ILNP are to allow much
functionality, such as IP-level mobility, to be
realised purely end-to-end, without new network
entities (e.g.  proxies, middleboxes, and tunnels),
and without additional routing state in the network.
This means that control of the operation of
functionality, such as IP-level mobility, remains at
the network edge, at the site network, and ultimately,
within end-systems.

However, for backwards compatibility with existing
infrastructure and for allowing incremental deployment,
ILNP is implemented in Linux by:
- (a) allowing existing applications to operate without
modification over the current sockets API; and
- (b) by having a "wire image" for packets that
is the same as IPv6.

Most of the work done on ILNP since the publication of
RFCs 6740-6748 has been on Linux. This talk will
describe the ILNP architecture, as well as the
functionality of an implementation of ILNP in the Linux
kernel, including results of testbed experiments for
IP-level mobility.

How does ILNP compare to ILA?

- The ILNP control plane currently is only needed for
situations where the Locator is updated, e.g. movement,
dynamic multihoming (no external databases as in ILA,
only the simple end-to-end handshake of RFC-6743)
no modifications to IPv6 routeing are required (no
I/L-specific routers, such as ILA routers, forwarding
and routeing is as for IPv6 as described in
RFC-6740/41)

- name resolution from FQDN to I/L values is via DNS
directly (no I -> L mapping system required as in ILA,
only the DNS RRs defined in RFC6742, which are already
implemented in BIND, KnotDNS, and NSD)

So, the infrastructure to support ILNP already exists,
and only end-system updates are required.

Kernel patches are currently on top of 4.9. We plan
to update and push upstream. The changes will be
described in the talk.

sessions.title: Designing sockets for U-LPWA wireless technologies
sessions.listing_title: Designing sockets for U-LPWA wireless technologies
sessions.description:
Low-Power Wide Area Network (LPWAN) wireless
technologies sacrifice data throughput for long-range
communication with long battery lifetime - Internet of
Things without Internet technologies. Linux comes into
play primarily for indoor and outdoor gateways from
U-LPWAN to Ethernet, Wifi or LTE, but also end nodes
may - in times of Raspberry Pi & Co. - be running
Linux. In 2018 the case has been made for a project to
bring LoRa PHY sockets into the kernel, with LoRaWAN
MAC layered on top. More and more cross-connections to
other LPWA or WPA network technologies have surfaced
during development.

This talk will give an update on where the discussions
have gone for LoRa, FSK, etc., with focus on netlink
layer, protocol families and socket addresses. Purpose
of the talk will be to spark discussions across
technology sub-communities (including also IEEE
802.15.4 and Bluetooth) on how to efficiently deal with
on-boarding a whole bunch of interconnected wireless
technologies, with a view to alignment and potential
reuse. Open topics include how to deal with multi-mode
chipsets, coexistence of hard-MAC stacks on hardware
modules (incl. Sigfox), firmware adding non-standard
MAC headers, incorporating sub-GHz regulatory
restrictions, layering a protocol stack with regards to
net_devices and SDR impacting design for wireless
drivers.

sessions.description:
The Linux kernel has successfully made its way across
datacenter top-of-rack switches, but these switches
live in a relatively sane and friendly environment.
Campus distribution and access switches however need
to deal with a much more hostile environment.

This paper intends to collate the currently relevant
features, give some operational context, and suggest
implementation strategies.

Among the collated topics are storm control, extended
validation and snooping features (SAVI), non-STP
loop protection, the MRP protocol family, and some
neighbor management excursions.

sessions.title: DUALPI2 - Low Latency, Low Loss and Scalable (L4S) AQM
sessions.listing_title: DUALPI2 - Low Latency, Low Loss and Scalable (L4S) AQM
sessions.description:
We implemented the ‘DUALPI2 AQM’ as a Linux qdisc, and
submitted the patch to the net-next mailing list. In
this talk, we would like to present the details of
DUALPI2 implementation and explain which problems it
can solve. The largest benefit of our solution is the
ability to deploy congestion controls like DCTCP on the
public Internet and allow a mix of DCTCP and Internet
congestion controls in the Data Center. The
standardization of the DualPI2 AQM and the way the Low
Latency, Low Loss and Scalable traffic (L4S) is
identified, are being finalized in the IETF.

Traditionally, classic loss-based congestion controls
like Cubic or Reno need a relatively “large” queue to
utilize the network efficiently and with reasonable
loss levels. These large queues introduce unnecessary
delay. Like in Data Centers, the problem can be
partially solved by using scalable congestion controls
that can use shallow immediate ECN marking thresholds
instead of loss as congestion signal. But then, another
problem is introduced - classic and scalable TCP
congestion controls are not able to coexist without
classic TCP starving itself. This starvation occurs due
to the difference in how classic and scalable
congestion controls respond to congestion signals. We
explain how DUALPI2 solves this problem and can be used
to mix Internet and Datacenter TCP traffic both on the
Internet and in Data Centers, without compromising on
neither the ultra-low latency performance of DCTCP, nor
the Reno/Cubic throughput performance. It uses a
scheduler with only 2 queues, coupled for fairness, and
a classifier that uses only IP header inspection, being
transport protocol independent (supporting TCP, SCTP,
QUIC, …).

sessions.title: Bottlenecks in increasing network speeds
sessions.listing_title: Bottlenecks in increasing network speeds
sessions.description:
Increasing NIC speeds come with new challenges and
bottlenecks.
Bottlenecks can appear starting from a critical rate,
and we need to identify them and prepare accordingly.

In this talk, I'm going to review the main bottlenecks
that were/are being addressed to support NIC speeds of
100Gbps, 200Gbps, and beyond.

The packet rate of a 200 Gbps NIC can be simulated on a
100 Gbps NIC, by using the simple technique of cutting
the MTU size by half.

One major bottleneck to present is the page allocation
rate.
I summarize several ideas and solutions that address
it:
[1] Page recycle, by maintaining a page cache
(in-driver cache, or page_pool).
[2] SKB remote release, avoid accesses to the
zone->lock by returning the SKB's pages directly into
the originating core's PCP,
[3] Optimise the common case of order-0 page
allocations in buddy system,
[4] Increase the buddy's scaling abilities by reducing
contention on the zone->lock.

Another bottleneck is hitting the PCI bandwidth.
A significant fraction of the PCI bandwidth might be
saved by reducing the packets descriptors overhead.

I will review innovative HW capabilities that reduce
the descriptors overhead, which made us reach a
milestone packet rate of 100 Million PPS in the XDP_TX
benchmark, and 135 Million PPS in XDP_DROP.
This includes HW features like:
[1] RX multi-packet descriptors,
[2] TX multi-packet descriptors,
[3] Compression of completion descriptors.
A standard API for configuring and controlling the
features is needed here, and is worth a discussion.

In addition, I will review general HW offload ideas,
that reduce the load on the CPUs.

sessions.title: An Asynchronous Dataplane for FRR
sessions.listing_title: An Asynchronous Dataplane for FRR
sessions.description:
The FRR (Free-range Routing) software suite has
historically been composed of single-threaded daemons,
each running a synchronous event loop.  Recent work
has begun migrating the FRR 'Zebra' daemon which
is responsible for maintaining the RIB and
programming the FIB, to a multithreaded
async design.

The asynchronous approach for FIB programming creates
an independent pthread which interacts with the kernel
via netlink. The system-call-focused task represents
the bulk of the work performed by the Zebra daemon
under load. We will describe how we take advantage of
new netlink features that improve scalability.
We will also introduce FRR support where the
forwarding plane resides a remote device.

In this talk we will describe the work and
challenges involved in achieving this goal.
We will describe the current state of
this work, present some initial results,
and discuss plans for the future.

sessions.title: Conntrack: tales of software datapaths
sessions.listing_title: Conntrack: tales of software datapaths
sessions.description:
Interest in offloading ConnTrack out of the core
networking stack is increasing. Conntrack is heavily
used by projects like OpenStack and the lack of its
offloading is hindering the adoption of OvS offloading.

This talk will be split in two parts.
First, we will cover our attempt on integrating
ConnTrack with TC in software datapath, which is used
by OvS for offloading and is a prerequisite for the hw
offloading.
We will show how it works, the challenges that we had
like the need for tc deferred actions, how we are
testing it and some preliminary performance numbers.
Next we will cover eBPF extensions for integrating with
ConnTrack. These are experimental changes that allow
eBPF programs to access the ConnTrack metadata. There
are a few possible ways we are looking at integrating
ConnTrack and eBPF. We will show one implementation of
this, and some performance numbers.

sessions.title: Viscum: A New Light Weight Architecture of Mobile Edge Computing
sessions.listing_title: Viscum: A New Light Weight Architecture of Mobile Edge Computing
sessions.description:
Multi-access edge computing (MEC), recently introduced
by ETSI industry Specification Group (ISG), is a
network architecture that offers cloud-computing
capabilities within the RAN or core network in the
cellular world to allow processing of tasks closer to
the cellular customer. It has, however, evolved to be
generic to apply to any network for deploying
applications and services as well as to store and
process content in close proximity to mobile users.

Current MEC solutions require either:
 a) deploying a specialized (often proprietary)
    mobile edge platform
or
 b) modifying existing applications (known as
    application splitting).

In this paper, we first review the current MEC
architecture introduced by ISG, and then propose an
alternative light weight mobile edge computing
architecture which utilizes existing Linux
kernel mechanisms, namely: Traffic Control (TC)
utilities, and network Namespaces.

Our solution is able to:
  i) deploy real-time applications onto mobile edge
     device without any modification to meet their low
     latency requirements;
 ii) provide computational offloading from either
     battery powered mobile devices or back end
     services in cloud;
iii) potentially convert any Linux based network devices
     (e.g. Wifi router, eNodeB) into application server
     without introducing new hardware.

The talk will go into details on how the Linux facilities
are used.

sessions.title: XDP based DDoS Mitigation
sessions.listing_title: XDP based DDoS mitigation
sessions.description:
XDP and eBPF provide a high performance mechanism for
packet processing, making it well suited for dropping
unwanted incoming packets. Cloudflare’s latest DDoS
mitigation system is using XDP to routinely handle
attacks of hundreds of gigabits per second across our
edge network. To date, we have seen single servers drop
over 11 million attack packets per second.

This talk will focus on the implementation of our XDP
solution, which automatically generates eBPF code to
respond to attacks. We will cover:

- Packet sampling with perf events to feed our attack
detection system, and its performance
- Using classic BPF as an intermediate representation
for our mitigation filters, and converting them to eBPF
- Load-time eBPF ELF configuration using relocation
info to enable us to compile once and run everywhere
- Automatic eBPF code generation and handling eBPF
verifier complexity limits
- Runtime performance

sessions.title: Implementing the 'TCP Prague' Requirements for L4S
sessions.listing_title: Implementing the 'TCP Prague' Requirements for L4S
sessions.description:
This talk is about a new approach for ultra-low queuing
delay that is intended to incrementally replace best
efforts as the default service of the public Internet.
Unlike traditional QoS, it's ultimately for all
traffic. In practice 'ultra-low queuing' means a few
hundred microseconds of queuing delay on average, and
about 1ms at the 99th percentile. This is 10 to 100
times better than the state-of-the-art AQMs (fq_CoDel
and PIE), which is achieved by addressing the root
cause of the problem - the congestion controller at the
source.

The solution is to use one of the family of 'scalable'
congestion controls. The talk will explain what that
means, but for now it will suffice to say that Data
Centre TCP (DCTCP) is an example. So the task has been
to make it possible and safe to incrementally deploy
congestion controls like DCTCP over the public
Internet.

The whole architecture is called Low Latency Low Loss
Scalable throughput (L4S). Although this all sounds
rather grandiose, it actually only involves a few
incremental changes to code in hosts and network nodes.
You will recognise some of these, because most are
desirable in themselves, and already in progress (e.g.
Accurate ECN and RACK). However, focusing on all the
parts loses sight of the sum. So this talk starts by
explaining the sum of the parts - the bigger motivation
for all the changes together.

The basic idea has been to build on the component parts
of DCTCP both in hosts and in queues. However, until
now, DCTCP could only be deployed in controlled
environments like DCs, because it would starve existing
Internet traffic. This 'coexistence problem' has been
solved by the DualQ Coupled AQM, which can be
incrementally deployed at bottlenecks. The IETF has
written a spec for this, and a qdisc called DualPI2
implements it, the details of which warrant a separate
talk.

Back in summer 2015, after a demonstration of
cloud-rendered interactive video over DCTCP over a
broadband access link running the DualQ Coupled AQM,
30-odd DCTCP-folks got together during the IETF in
Prague and agreed a prioritized set of changes to DCTCP
that would be needed to deploy it over the public
Internet. The list was dubbed the 'TCP Prague
requirements', which were subsequently written into an
IETF spec.

This talk introduces the important components of the
first 'TCP Prague' implementation to satisfy these
requirements, which have been open-sourced in Linux. As
well as giving rationale and explanation, it explains
how the parts integrate together, both within each
system and at Internet scale, and outlines the maturity
of each component implementation, plus some points of
interest and issues where decisions are needed.

sessions.title: IPsec encapsulation over TCP
sessions.listing_title: IPsec encapsulation over TCP
sessions.description:
One issue with using IPsec is that middleboxes may
interfere with UDP traffic required to configure it
with IKE (Internet Key Exchange Protocol). To work
around this problem, RFC 8229 proposes to encapsulate
IPsec and IKE traffic over a TCP connection, which
middleboxes are more likely to let through.

This talk will introduce the encapsulation mechanism
over standard TCP connections, describe the
implementation I'm proposing, which relies on existing
kernel infrastructure (TCP upper layer protocol
mechanism (ULP) and stream parser), and how it can be
used by userspace IKE daemons.

This work is based on a previous proposal by Herbert
Xu: 
https://patchwork.ozlabs.org/patch/859110/
https://patchwork.ozlabs.org/patch/859109/

sessions.listing_title: Performance Study of NVMe/TCP and NVMe/RoCE on Linux
sessions.description:
Support for running NVMe over Fabrics (NVMe-oF) using
the TCP transport protocol was recently added to Linux.
This makes it possible to run NVMe-oF in environments
where RDMA is not supported due to its NIC hardware
requirements, the requirements it imposes on the
fabric, or other constraints. Obviously, a performance
impact is expected when using TCP instead of an RDMA
transport such as RoCE.

This session describes a performance study comparing
NVMe/TCP to NVMe/RoCE on Linux. Throughput, latency
distribution, and CPU load are measured and compared. A
performance comparison of these kernel protocols to
user-level protocols using SPDK will also be described.

sessions.listing_title: The Core Cost of Doing Business
sessions.description:
Achieving line-rate reception or transmission of flows
with the Linux kernel datapath often seems trivial with
technologies like LRO, GRO, and TSO. However, when
forwarding traffic using the Linux kernel datapath there
is often a greater cost per packet to make sure it
arrives at its intended destination -- whether that
destination is a VM, container, or a remote system.
This talk will cover in detail:

- the cost of the kernel datapath forwarding operation
- the typical cost of the destination lookup of a packet
  including how forwarding table state impacts lookup
  speed
- the impact of the size of the frames on link
  utilization

The goal will be to present a formula for estimating the
minimum number of server cores that will be needed to
service traffic at particular rates and frame sizes
for IPv4 and IPv6 as well and VxLAN encapsulated
or tunneled traffic with the goal of understanding how
the utilization of these cores impacts planning and
deployment of new systems.

sessions.title: AF_GRAFT: A new address family for containerized applications
sessions.listing_title: AF_GRAFT: A new address family for containerized applications
sessions.description:
Current container networking model is derived from the
traditional networking model based on interfaces and
links. Network stacks of a host and a container are
separated instances connected by a virtual link
(usually veth). Therefore, packets from the container
pass through the two network stacks, so that network
performance degrades in comparison with native hosts
involving a single network stack.

As an approach for mitigating this overhead, we propose
a new data communication channel design, called
AF_GRAFT, for containers. Instead of the link between
the host and container network stacks, AF_GRAFT
provides a socket-layer interconnection between them.
An application on a container opens sockets by
socket(AF_GRAFT, SOCK_STREAM, 0) for instance, and
bind() grafts the sockets onto proper sockets opened on
the host network stack across the network namespace
boundary. As a result, the containerize application
obtains comparable throughput and latency with native
hosts by bypassing the container network stack.

This talk introduces AF_GRAFT and its kernel module
implementation, a tool to run existing applications
with AF_GRAFT, and a demonstration of simple
integration with docker.

sessions.title: NVMe over TCP/IP
sessions.listing_title: NVMe over TCP/IP
sessions.description:
NVMe over Fabrics is a powerful standard that provides
fast access to non-volatile memory devices across
different fabric interconnects. An emerging NVMe-oF
transport is good old TCP/IP. Its benefits are obvious, as
it is fast, scalable, well-understood, and extremely
simple to deploy. TCP/IP is, after all, the most widely
used network protocol of them all, and well known and
heavily-implemented in every data center.

The NVMe Technical Working Group has built both the
standard and its open-source implementation in concert.
Its prominent features include data integrity and
transport layer security. In practice, NVMe/TCP is an
excellent transport for networked flash and complements
NVMe/RDMA and NVMe/FC nicely.

This session will:
- introduce NVMe, NVMe over Fabrics (NVMe-oF), NVMe-oF
  over TCP (NVMe/TCP)
- present the Linux implementation and go over its details
- solicit feedback on some of the outstanding issues

sessions.title: XDP offload with virtio-net
sessions.listing_title: XDP offload with virtio-net
sessions.description:
This talk will describe offloading eBPF/XDP from guest
VM to host through co-operation between the host
and guest.
The goal is to run and accelerate the guest VM 
network and bring it to par with host speed.

The talk will cover:

1. Brief review of eBPF/XDP and its hardware offload
   support

2. The need and use cases of XDP offload through
   virtio-net

3. The design and implementation:

- virtio extension to support passing eBPF program
  and map action.
- eBPF/XDP offload infrastructure support for
  virtio-net XDP offload.
- eBPF/XDP offload and its migration support in Qemu.
- Host TUN/TAP support for offloaded XDP program.
- XDP offload in normal skb path.

4. Performance numbers
5. Challenges and security implication
6. Future work

sessions.title: Skb Meta Data Extensions
sessions.listing_title: Skb Meta Data Extensions
sessions.description:
This talk is a deep-dive into the inner workings of the
recently added skb extension infrastructure.
skb extensions are designed to allow subsystems
(e.g. bridge netfilter) that are not used in common
setups to associate data with an sk_buff in a way that
does not increase the size of the sk_buff structure.

skb extensions achieve this by keeping the extra data in
a separate memory area that is allocated only when needed.
This memory region is free'd automatically by kfree_skb.
After an overview of the general concept, the talk will
elaborate on a few implementation choices, explain
constraints and limitations of the infrastructure, cover
intended future use cases (Multipath tcp) and in what
situations it might make sense to (re)use this
infrastructure.

For more information, please see:
upstream commit

sessions.title: Devlink health reporting and recovery system
sessions.listing_title: Devlink health reporting and recovery system
sessions.description:
The Devlink health mechanism is targeted for Real Time
Alerting to indicate when something bad happens to a
PCI device. The goals are:
- to provide alert debug information
- To provide self healing
- If the problem needs vendor support, provide a way to
gather all needed debugging information.

The main idea is to unify and centralize driver health
reports in the generic devlink instance and allow the
user to set different attributes of the health reporting
and recovery procedures.

The devlink health reporter:
Device driver creates a "health reporter" per each
error/health type.  Error/Health type can be a
known/generic (eg pci error, fw error, rx/tx error) or
unknown (driver specific).
For each registered health reporter, a driver can issue
error/health reports asynchronously. All health report
handling is done by devlink.
Device drivers can provide specific callbacks for each
"health reporter", e.g.
- Recovery procedures
- Diagnostics and object dump procedures
- OOB initial attributes
Different parts of the driver can register different
types of health reporters with different handlers.

Once an error is reported, devlink health will do the
following actions:
* issue a log to send to the kernel trace events buffer
* update Health status and statistics for the
reporter instance
* Object dump is taken and saved at the reporter
instance (as long as there is no other dump which is
already stored)
* Auto recovery attempt is made. Depends on:
  - Auto-recovery configuration
  - Grace period vs. time passed since last recover

The user interface:
-------------------
User can access/change each reporter's attributes and
driver specific callbacks via devlink, e.g per error
type (per health reporter)
- Configure reporter's generic attributes (like:
  Disable/enable auto recovery)
- Invoke recovery procedure
- Run diagnostics
- Object dump

The devlink health interface commands (via netlink):
DEVLINK_CMD_HEALTH_REPORTER_GET
  Retrieves status and configuration info per DEV and
  reporter.
DEVLINK_CMD_HEALTH_REPORTER_SET
  Allows reporter-related configuration setting.
DEVLINK_CMD_HEALTH_REPORTER_RECOVER
  Triggers a reporter's recovery procedure.
DEVLINK_CMD_HEALTH_REPORTER_DIAGNOSE
  Retrieves diagnostics data from a reporter on a device.
DEVLINK_CMD_HEALTH_REPORTER_DUMP_GET
  Retrieves the last stored dump. Devlink health
  saves a single dump. If an dump is not already stored by
  the devlink for this reporter, devlink generates a new
  dump.
  dump output is defined by the reporter.
DEVLINK_CMD_HEALTH_REPORTER_DUMP_CLEAR
  Clears the last saved dump file for the specified
  reporter.

iproute2), example:

$> devlink health show pci/0000:00:09.0 reporter TX \
   pci/0000:00:09.0:

name TX state healthy #err 0 #recover 1 last_dump_ts N/A
dump_available false attributes:
grace period 600 auto recover true

sessions.title: P4 Compiler Backend for TC
sessions.listing_title: P4 Compiler Backend for TC
sessions.description:
This talk will describe an architecture of modern
switching ASICs with an emphasis on their
programmability and how it can be used in Linux through
traffic control(TC). The details of a P4 to TC
compiler with switchdev as the HW backend will be
described.

The goal for having this type of compiler is to make
possible programming Linux pipeline with P4, which is
more user-friendly and widely accepted by ASIC vendors.

The talk will cover:
1. Overview of programmable switching ASICs
2. Linux TC as a P4 target architecture
3. The P4 TC backend design and implementation:
- Compiler architecture
- TC as the standard Linux backend
- Switchdev HW offload
- Current state
4. Use case
5. Future work

sessions.title: De-mystifying the networking relationship with Kubernetes
sessions.listing_title: De-mystifying the networking relationship with Kubernetes
sessions.description:
This tutorial will focus on networking Linux Containers
using the Container Network Interface (CNI) and
Kubernetes (k8s). Details of how the various pieces of
Kubernetes networking in Linux and the challenges they
present will be covered:

The container network model will be described with
emphasis on how it differs from VMs.
A brief overview of what Kubernetes (k8s) is and how it
uses containers and the Container Networking Interface
(CNI) will be given.
CNI itself, how containers change networking
expectations, and some of the problems encountered will
be described.
Finally, using the Multus CNI plugin to work around k8s
networking limitations will be explained.

time left for Q&A.

sessions.title: Netlink Workshop
sessions.listing_title: Netlink Workshop
sessions.description:
The Goal of this workshop is to discuss Linux kernel
Netlink API development. Discussion will include:

Netlink Overview:

 - references to rtnetlink and genl
 - Netlink groups and ids > 31 (exceeding 32-bit bitfield)
Recent updates - status of changes over the last few years

 - extack : improving user experience with better messages
 - kernel side filtering : reducing the amount of data
   sent to userspace
 - reducing notifications - e.g., ipv6 route delete
   notifications
 - strict get requests - rigid checking of data in requests
   enabling future filters
 - Johannes’ policy changes

Problems/Challenges

 - Growth of attributes and impacts to stack memory use
 - Past mistakes/shortsightedness and impacts to future
   changes requiring ugly workarounds in the API. Need
   to be better about APIs.
 - Recent efforts to address

Performance

 - Batching notifications?
 - Kernel side filtering of dump requests
     - reducing data sent to userspace
     - this point forward requires strict dump checks
 - BPF
     - using socket filters
     - extension to eBPF and applying filters earlier

  - Reducing notifications
        - reference IPv4 route delete, option for IPv6
        - can we have a bool per netlink group that
          signals no listener for the notifications so
          don’t generate them?

Networking APIs that need to be converted to netlink

 - Ethtool: move to netlink, challenges
   (Michal Kubecek to discuss)

Hardware offload

 - Devlink (Jiri Pirko - summary of the existing state,
   extensions and challenges)
Lack of Documentation

We invite input for additional topics to discuss.

sessions.title: TCP Analytics
sessions.listing_title: TCP Analytics
sessions.description:
Participants:
Neal Cardwell, Yuchung Cheng, Soheil Hassas Yeganeh,
Lawrence Brakmo, Eric Dumazet, Chris Rapier,
Jamal Hadi Salim, Jason Baron, Jae Won Chung

There are numerous cases of TCP performance challenges and 
anomalies reported in production environments that are very
hard to debug, raising an interest in the answer to the 
question "how to monitor TCP flows efficiently".

The workshop will constitute the sharing of experience from
folks who deal with TCP Analytics Extraction at very large
TCP deployments from several organizations. Discussions will
include descriptions of the instrumentation used at these 
organizations, the motivation behind these diagnostics,
and ways to improve/enhance this as we go forward

A sample of the topics of interest that we hope to discuss
are listed below. Note that the list below is a
work-in-progress, and we do invite input for additional
interesting topics to discuss. The agenda will get more
clarity as the conference dates approach.

- walk-through of tcp_info instrumentation including (but
not restricted to) Tx and Rx timestamps along with
OPT_STATS (including TCP chronos TCP_NLA_BUSY,
TCP_NLA_RWND_LIMITED, ...) that we have upstreamed.
Those are crucial for us in debugging production
performance issues. A description of the motivation,
use-cases that it solves for Google, some of the gotchas
about the semantics will be shared

- Similar discussion around tcp-bpf; discussion of recent
patches to tcp-bpf infra to get asynchronous notifications
of interesting TCP connections- how to evolve these as we go
forward

- Akamai tcpstats interface for collecting TCP connection
statistics.

sessions.title: Workshop on IoT related MAC layers, header compressions and routing protocols
sessions.listing_title: Workshop on IoT related MAC layers, header compressions and routing protocols
sessions.description:
This workshop serves for follow up discussions and
status updates on similar workshops we have been
running in earlier NetDev conference editions. It will
continue on topics discussed and bring new ones on the
table.

A rough idea on the agenda can be found below. The final
one depends on who can attend and input from the
attendees. We will post the final agenda closer to the
conference date:

-ieee802154 and 6lowpan subsystems (status update, netlink
-API to configure 6lowpan, kselftest)
-LoRa subsystem (report on ongoing work
and blockers for merging)
-Bluetooth (status update, Bluetooth mesh,
version 5 features)
-RPL implementations for Linux (unstrung, other
implementaions, needed kernel interfaces)

This workshop in general aims to identify generic
requirements for the networking subsystem for IoT and
starting the process of addressing the gaps found. The
workshop will encompass related MAC layers, networking
protocols, adaptation layers, header compression,
routing protocols and application layers.

sessions.title: Open Source, the IETF, and You
sessions.listing_title: Open Source, the IETF, and You
sessions.description:
Sometimes open source and open standards are cast as
adversaries: if you have a decent open source
implementation, what do you need a standardized
specification for? On the Internet today we have a
range of different models for how open source and open
standards co-exist, many of which are mutually
supportive. This talk will use two IETF standardization
efforts, TLS 1.3 and QUIC, to demonstrate the benefits
of having a tight feedback loop between open source
development and standards development. These efforts
will also be used to reflect about ossification in
Internet protocols and how it is being addressed in the
IETF. Attendees will be encouraged to think about how
the Linux developer community and the IETF community
might work more closely together on this and other
challenges.

opportunity to network between attendees, sponsors,

accompanying them to the conference (family members 
etc. don't have to be registered). We just ask that
if you are bringing someone just let the registration
desk know when you pick your badge so we can plan
better for food and drinks.

recruiting. We will also provide a table for any
project that is open to make attendees aware of their
work (we will send out a separate note requesting open
source projects to request for space).
